title: By deeds
hookLine: a man shouts 'outcast!' at the Buddha, and gets a question back
carry: what someone does, not where they're from

lines: A SACRED FIRE, READY AND PURE.
cards: Morning in the city of Savatthi. In one house a brahmin named Aggika Bharadvaja has his sacred fire burning and his offerings laid out, everything ready and pure. Down the street with his alms bowl comes the Buddha.
To this man, at this moment, a shaven-headed wanderer near his fire is a kind of pollution. So he shouts. Stop there, shaveling!
Stop there, you wretched monk! Stop there, outcast! There are two easy moves next: shout back, or walk away hurt.

teach.h: DO YOU KNOW WHAT AN OUTCAST IS?
teach.b: He asks a question. Do you know, brahmin, what an outcast is, or what makes someone one? The brahmin, maybe surprised, says: no, I don't.
Teach me. So the Buddha does, in verse. In the brahmin's mouth, vasala, outcast, is an insult about birth: a word for someone low, someone whose presence stains.
The Buddha keeps the word and changes what earns it. Whoever is angry and holds grudges is an outcast. Whoever harms living beings.
Whoever steals, or borrows money and then denies the debt. Whoever lies as a witness. Whoever is able to support aging parents and doesn't.
Whoever strikes or insults their family. Whoever does wrong and hopes no one will find out. Whoever praises themselves and looks down on others.
Then he tells of Matanga, a candala's son, born into a group his society kept at the bottom, who became so renowned that nobles and brahmins came to serve him. His birth didn't stop him.
Then the line: not by birth is one an outcast, not by birth is one a brahmin. By deeds one becomes an outcast; by deeds one becomes a brahmin. And look at the scene.

teach.h: ANGRY, CRUEL, LOOKING DOWN ON OTHERS
teach.b: The list is long, and the man who just shouted is standing right there, angry, looking down on someone.
He describes it, and lets the brahmin find himself in it.
At the end, the brahmin asks to become a follower.

how: The Vasala Sutta is chanted as one of the protective discourses in Theravada communities, and Buddhists speaking about dignity and caste quote its line, not by birth, by deeds.

o: by what you do, not by birth
by the family you were born into
by the offerings made at the fire

games.q: the outcast discourse: tap the pairs.
p: do you know what an outcast is?

s: the Buddha shouts back at the brahmin
he answers with a question: do you know what makes an outcast?
the list of outcast deeds includes failing to support aging parents
along with anger, cruelty, theft, lying and looking down on others.
the brahmin stays angry and sends him away
at the end he asks to become a follower.

games.q: you're walking with your bowl. a man by his fire shouts: stop there, outcast! what does the Buddha do?
o: ask him: do you know what an outcast is?
turn and leave without a word.
games.why: he answers with a question, then a teaching: not by birth, by deeds.

practice: Think of someone people tend to overlook or look down on, the person who empties the bins, the new kid, the neighbor nobody greets, and see them clearly.
Recall one good deed you've seen them do, or could imagine them doing, and let that deed, not their place, be what you see.

wordCard.voice: By deeds. The Buddha's answer to the brahmin who called him an outcast: no one is low or noble by birth, only by what they do. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kammuna: by action, by deeds (from kamma). the key word in 'by deeds one becomes an outcast'.

carryVoice: Your line: what someone does, not where they're from. Birth was never the measure. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.7, Vasala Sutta (also called Aggika Bharadvaja Sutta)
Sutta Nipata 3.9, Vasettha Sutta (the same refrain)
